nodes.label: Automatic Water Level Control System
nodes.rationale: Chosen because the PDF emphasizes basic control concepts over a sophisticated system; only water level matters so no volume or area is calculated.

nodes.label: Open-Loop Mode (Timed)
nodes.rationale: Fixed pre-calculated run time t_run = r / K-hat_h, so reliance on a model alone can be compared with feedback.

nodes.label: Closed-Loop Mode (On-Off)
nodes.rationale: Pump runs until the measured level rise reaches the target, so the result does not depend on the estimated pump rate.

nodes.label: On-Off Control Law
nodes.rationale: A simple bang-bang law is used instead of a tuned PID because the course focuses on basic feedback concepts; with an integrating plant the level holds once the pump stops.

nodes.label: Level Rise Equation y = d0 - d
nodes.rationale: The sensor is treated as unity gain on level because 1 cm of level change reads as 1 cm; the glass area is never needed.

nodes.label: Sensor Resolution Limitation (+/-0.3 cm)
nodes.rationale: The HC-SR04 is good to about +/-3 mm, which becomes +/-0.3 cm of level uncertainty because the output is the level itself; about 10 percent of a 3 cm target and 5 percent of a 6 cm target.

nodes.label: Optocoupler Isolation and Separate Grounds
nodes.rationale: Isolation keeps pump switching noise away from the Nano and HC-SR04; a relay was rejected for wear and no PWM slowdown, and IRF520/L298N for weak logic-level drive and voltage drop.

nodes.label: Straight-Sided Glass Requirement
nodes.rationale: A tapered glass makes the level rise rate change with height, breaking the constant-rate model; a straight-sided glass keeps K_h constant and the area need not be measured.

nodes.label: Plant Transfer Function G(s) = Kh / (s(tau s + 1))
nodes.rationale: Plant split into a first-order pump/tubing lag in series with a glass integrator; the integrator means the level holds its value when the pump stops.

nodes.label: Disturbance Test (Pinched Tube / Height Change)
nodes.rationale: A pinched tube is preferred over weak batteries because a pack below the module minimum can make the pump switch erratically rather than just run slower, which would not match the model.

nodes.label: Wokwi Controller Simulation
nodes.rationale: Wokwi has no pump or glass, so the software plant model (SIMULATE 1) replaces the sensor reading with computed level rise and shows the pump as an LED on D9.

nodes.label: SIM_GAIN Disturbance (Pump 20 Percent Weaker)
nodes.rationale: SIM_GAIN = 0.8 models the real pump as 20 percent weaker than the estimate so the open-loop vs closed-loop difference can be shown without hardware.

nodes.label: Open-Loop Trusts the Model, Closed-Loop Trusts the Measurement
nodes.rationale: Core design lesson: a model-based timed controller is accurate only when the real rate matches the estimate, whereas a measured-output controller is robust to rate changes.

nodes.label: Bench Test Order (One Component at a Time)
nodes.rationale: Testing each part alone means a failure always points to one thing; one component and one small sketch at a time avoids ambiguous whole-system failures.

nodes.label: Scope and Limitations
nodes.rationale: Fundamental concepts over sophistication: low-voltage supply, straight-sided glass, on-off controller only, no volume calculation, drain pump excluded to limit cost and risk.

nodes.label: Chapter 2: System Design and Mathematical Model
Isolated Driver Design Decision
nodes.rationale: Battery negative is not joined to Nano ground so pump switching noise stays away from the Nano and sensor; a separate 4xAA pack ensures the pump never runs from an Arduino pin or USB power.
